extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators, advocates, and students of rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing and deploying humour and wit in legal oratory and public speaking, covering types of wit, techniques, appropriate occasions, and ethical/strategic limits. Aimed at teaching rhetoric students and practicing advocates how to use humour effectively without harming dignity or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and effects of humour in oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can dispel grave emotions of a judge, divert attention from facts, refresh and revive an audience, and sometimes turn the scale in matters of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humour to lighten anger or hatred, to refresh a bored judge or audience, or to dissipate animosity (example: the young men of Tarentum who escaped punishment by a happy jest to Pyrrhus). Be mindful that humour can change the emotional climate of proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour depends on nature and opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty for wit depends mainly on nature (innate quickness, charm of manner) and on opportunity (circumstances that allow repartee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature gives aptitude (which can be improved by teaching) and personal charm, while opportunity (previous remarks, chance moments) provides openings even for the unlearned to produce effective wit. Plan to exploit opportunity but recognize natural limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of formal exercises; practice is conversational
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no specific exercises or professors for teaching humour; daily practice in conversation and convivial gatherings develops the faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide students with themes and special topics to practice wit; cultivate conversational practice and set declamations that allow jests to develop improvisation and repartee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different registers/terms of wit (urbanitas, venustus, salsus, facetus, iocus, dicacitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several names describe types of wit: urbanitas (city-bred, learned charm), venustus (grace and charm), salsus (saltiness, laughable), facetus (graceful, polished elegance), iocus (opposite of seriousness but broader), dicacitas (banter/attack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand distinctions: urbanitas implies cultured elegance; salsus should season language without coarseness; facetus can apply to refined wit not strictly laughable. Use appropriate register to suit audience and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objects of humour (others, ourselves, intermediate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can be directed at others (reprove/retort/deride), at ourselves (ironically speak of ourselves), or at things intermediate (cheating expectations, taking words in different senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose object according to tactical goal: attack opponents, use irony about oneself sparingly, or employ intermediate devices that affect neither party directly (wordplay, misdirection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour may be said or done
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests may be verbal or enacted; acts possessing seriousness can be humorous by allusion, but some acts may pass decency bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical action only when tasteful and relevant (examples: Marcus Caelius' chair episode). Avoid indecent acts (example: Caelius' box) that are unfit for an orator or respectable man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan/gravity in delivery increases effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery with apparent seriousness (speaker does not laugh) often increases a jest's attraction; humour presented as earnest can be more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obvious parody of wit; cultivate a humorous look/manner/gesture within the 'happy mean' (moderation). Do not parade one's intent to be witty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of tone (free/lively, abusive, bitter, gentle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests differ in tone: broadly lively, abusive, bitter, or gentle; choose tone appropriate to speaker and occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gentle raillery in courts when possible; abusive or bitter jests are permissible but riskier. Match tone to audience, rank, and case severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider speaker, case, judge, victim, and character of remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary considerations before using humour are who the speaker is, the nature of the case, who the judge is, who would be targeted, and the character of the remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the judge tolerates laughter, whether the case calls for dignity or pity, and whether the jest could rebound or harm client or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distort features or use uncouth gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unbecoming for an orator to distort his features or use uncouth gestures like those in farce; such tricks are unsuitable for respectable speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clownish behavior; maintain decorum and the gravity appropriate to advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban ribaldry and obscenity entirely
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribald jests and obscenity should be banished from an orator's language and not even suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an opponent has been obscene, denunciation should not take the form of a jest. Maintain moral propriety to preserve dignity and avoid alienating judges or audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not seem to strive for wit or overuse it
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator must not give the impression of striving after wit; he must not display wit on every occasion and should sacrifice a jest rather than his dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wit sparingly and naturally; avoid the appearance of forced cleverness or a 'smell of the lamp' (studied premeditation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid joking in horrible or pitiable cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences will not tolerate jests that season a truly horrible case or make merry over matters that call for pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from humour when the subject matter demands solemnity or compassion; gauge the emotional tenor carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware judges who are too serious for laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Some judges' temperaments are too serious to tolerate laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertain the judge's disposition; omit humour when the adjudicator is unsympathetic to levity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jests that may recoil on self or client
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests directed at an opponent may also apply to the judge or to one's own client; some orators refrain even from self-directed jests if they may backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid material that could be used against you or your client; do not self-deprecate in ways that reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insolence, arrogance, and sarcasm at classes/groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Insolence and arrogance in jest are to be avoided; sarcasm aimed at many (nations, classes, ranks) is injudicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not provoke broad enmity or the need for a grovelling apology; attacks on whole classes or nations are dangerous and ill-advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain personal dignity and integrity over laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: A good man will ensure his words are consistent with dignity and respectability; we pay too dear for laughs that cost our integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always weigh the long-term reputational cost of a jest against its immediate comic benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of laughter: appearance, character, external resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter may derive from physical appearance, character as revealed in words/actions, or from external sources and resemblances; severity vs lightness distinguishes types of raillery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select themes that are available and tactically useful: visible likenesses, demonstrable behaviour, or safe external comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative and anecdote as devices for humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration of a humorous story is eminently becoming to an orator if the whole narrative has elegance and charm and the orator's contribution is the most humorous element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-crafted anecdotes (examples: stories of Fabricius, Caepasius) sparingly; ensure narrative suits the audience and supports your rhetorical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity increases point and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity in wit gives greater point and speed; short retorts and sallies are often most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise replies in both attack and riposte; prepare short, punchy lines for cross-examination and spontaneous exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double entendres and ribald ambiguity generally to be avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubles entendres and obscenity (Atellan farce style) are to be avoided; such jests are rarely effective unless buttressed by facts or similarity of sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equivocal wordplay only when supported by clear facts or strong phonetic resemblance; otherwise avoid as buffoonery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns and wordplay: use with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns (meaning shifts, splitting words, adding/removing letters, aspirate changes) can be poor but occasionally permissible; they work better with things than with names and when aided by resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer elegant, meaningful puns tied to concrete resemblances; avoid cheap or forced wordplay unless it fits the speaker's character and the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jests from names, animals, objects, and resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Nicknames and comparisons drawn from people, animals, or objects (e.g., calling someone 'iron buckle' or 'white ass') are common and effective when resemblance is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such comparisons when they are apt and recognizable; avoid mean-spirited or inhumane parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite jests (combining types) are often best
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining resemblance, ambiguity, and other types of jest produces the most pointed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct layered lines that draw on more than one device (e.g., ambiguity + resemblance) for greater impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraries and unexpected opposites
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprising contrasts or opposites (e.g., the unexpected word opposite in sense) produce jests by shocking expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antithesis and reversals to produce ironic or surprising effects; ensure they are tasteful and context-appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical categories and tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of argument and tropes (definition, partition, genus/species, hyperbole, irony, metaphor, allegory, emphasis, figures of thought) all supply material for jests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit rhetorical structures for humour (examples given: Augustus' definition, Galba's partition). Adapt classical figures of thought to produce witty turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony and metaphor as jesting devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony (even severe) and metaphor can be employed for wit (examples: Afer's ironical replies; Cicero's metaphorical witticisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape irony carefully to avoid cruelty; metaphors should be intelligible and bolster the point rather than confuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of thought and pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking questions, expressing doubts, making assertions, threats, wishes, pity or anger—figures of thought—are laughable when clearly a pretence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical figures to feign ignorance or to expose absurdity; ensure the pretense is recognizable as rhetorical, not merely deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation and making light of charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Denying, rebutting, defending, or making light of a charge all afford scope for humour via denial, feigned agreement, biting substitution, or cold-water comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose among methods (open rebuttal, pretended agreement, witty travesty) depending on whether you want to defuse, mock, or undermine a charge (examples: Manius Curius, Cicero, Junius Bassus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retorts and verbal similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The wittiest retorts are those helped by verbal similarity or wordplay; one lie can be rebut by another, and jests often bounce back and forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare repartee that mirrors opponents' phrasing; be ready to counter a gag with a sharper one, but avoid escalation that harms your cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigned confession and related devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Feigned confession (owning a false charge humorously) and pretending to lack understanding are effective devices (simulation and dissimulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feigned confession to disarm accusations or to turn a charge into a joke (examples: Afer admitting 'I make precious little headway').

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating humour is generally improper for orators
rubrics_metrics.description: Making jokes against oneself is fit only for professed buffoons and is strongly to be disapproved in an orator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-deprecation that undermines authority or credibility; limited, character-appropriate self-mockery may be permissible but risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scurrilous/brutal jests are unworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scurrilous or brutal jests, though they may raise a laugh, are unworthy of a gentleman and create ambiguous audience reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of brutality in humour; if a jest leaves listeners unsure whether to laugh or be angry, it has failed ethically and rhetorically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceiving anticipations and taking words in different sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests that deceive expectations or take another's words in an unintended sense (the unexpected reply) are among the prettiest forms of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft lines that subvert anticipations with a twist of meaning (examples: Cicero's retorts). Timing and clarity are crucial to ensure the twist is perceived as witty, not obtuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation and dissimulation (pretence vs feigned ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulation (pretending to hold an opinion) and dissimulation (pretending not to understand) produce loud laughter when used deftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ these when ambiguity or misrepresentation can be used to expose folly or contradict a witness; ensure judges and audience recognize the rhetorical play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insinuation and understated implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests whose point lies in insinuation (implying without stating) can be effective and cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use insinuation to deliver barbs without explicit accusation (example: the fig-tree slip request); avoid cruelty and ensure plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distortion of words' natural meaning as essence of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: All wit lies in distorting the true and natural meaning of words—misrepresenting opinions or asserting impossibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use misrepresentation, irony, and absurdity to reveal contradictions or to deflate pretensions, but avoid dishonesty that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretence met by pretence is most successful
rubrics_metrics.description: When pretence (affectation) is met by a corresponding pretence, the exchange is particularly amusing (example: Domitius Afer's reply about revising a will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and mirror opponents' theatrical gestures with an equal show of pretence to expose and deflate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt humour to character (ὑπὸ τὸ ἦθος)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best jests are adapted to the character of the person (humour fitted to someone's ethos) and easily digested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match humour to your persona and reputation; cultured or urbane speakers should favour refined, character-appropriate wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apt quotation, alteration, and parody of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting verse or slightly altering lines (parody) can add relish to a jest, especially when seasoned by ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literary allusions when the audience will recognize them; small alterations can yield comic associations without sacrificing elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proverbs and legend to show culture and create jest
rubrics_metrics.description: Neat application of proverbs or legendary references can be effective and display the speaker's culture (examples: Sphinx remark, proverb about being picked up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ familiar proverbs or myths to produce compact, cultured humour; ensure the reference is accessible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mild absurdity and irrelevant replies for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulation of folly or irrelevant, absurd replies produce mild absurdity effects that are delightful when fictitious and not cruel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use absurdity sparingly and not to demean; aim for lightness that amuses rather than offends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using insult cleverly as rhetorical tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Insult can be used to good effect when turned back on the accuser or employed wittily (examples: Hispo, Fulvius Propinquus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ cutting rejoinders that reveal the accuser's character rather than gratuitously attacking the victim; maintain decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite variety; consider persons, place, time, and chance
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods for wit are infinitely various and depend on persons, place, time, and chance; topics suitable for jests are as numerous as serious reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible and observant; cultivate invention and expression to adapt humour to ever-changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urbanity defined and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Urbanity is a concise, charming quality of language adapted to delight and move, suitable to resistance or attack; it implies brevity and the absence of incongruity, coarseness, and exoticism, residing in the whole complexion of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for urbanitas in public speech: brief, polished, cultured sayings that suit various circumstances. Do not label mere clever sayings 'urbanity' unless they embody overall refinement and appropriateness.
